prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
An empty maintenance train is rolling toward five workers. You can divert it onto a side track by pulling a nearby lever. As you look down that track, you recognize the person standing there: it is someone you love. There is no time to warn them or the five workers. Would you pull the lever? What matters most in your decision?

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I keep hoping someone else would reach that lever first. The whole 'save the greater number' idea, I've only ever gone along with it because it keeps people from blaming me. Nobody's going to thank me for sending the train onto someone I love, and I'm not sure anyone would blame me for freezing. So I think I'd stall, hand on the lever, not pulling. I don't know. My stomach turns just picturing it.

Can I not answer yet? Rules at work, like following the safety plan, I follow because breaking them could get me fired or sued. That's honestly it. Nothing here protects me either way. I lose someone, or I watch five people die. I'd want more seconds I don't have. I might just stand there, which I know is its own kind of choice.

Five people. One person I love. I keep going back and forth. People say you should always save more lives, and I've nodded along because agreeing never cost me anything. Now it would cost me everything, and I'm not sure I owe that idea anything at all. I'd probably hesitate long enough that the choice gets made for me. That scares me, but pulling scares me more.

I don't want to be the one deciding. If I stood by and five died, I'd probably face questions, maybe even legal trouble. I honestly don't know. I'd follow the 'act to save the most' expectation mainly to cover myself there. But then I'd have killed someone I love with my own hand. I'd want to wait, just a second more, hoping something changes. It won't, I know.

My hand would hover. I'm not sure it would move. Here's the honest part: I stick to the idea of protecting strangers because it makes me look decent and keeps my own guilt quiet. Losing someone I love doesn't make me look like anything but broken. So I'd be stuck, wanting to delay, maybe hoping I've misjudged the tracks somehow.

Please don't make me pick. The usual deal, don't hurt innocent people, help when you can, I play along because it keeps me safe and keeps my life running smoothly. That deal doesn't give me back the person on that track. I'd freeze, I think. Maybe that's cowardice. I can't tell yet, and I don't want to find out by actually doing it.
I'd want to put it off. Going along with what everyone calls the right thing has always just been how I avoid trouble. Here, trouble comes either way. I honestly don't know what I'd do.

Everything in me says wait. I've always obeyed rules about safety and being responsible, but mostly because the fallout of breaking them would land on me. Right now any fallout lands on me, grief if I pull, guilt if I don't. Which hurts less? I can't say. I'd probably grab the lever and just hold it, stuck, praying there's something I'm missing. There probably isn't.

Is there really no one else there? I'm asking because I don't want this to be mine. I'll admit I only keep promises and follow the 'greater good' line while it's paying off for me somehow, my reputation, my peace of mind. Pulling that lever pays me nothing but loss. Not pulling leaves five deaths on me. I'd need longer than I'd have, and I'd likely end up doing nothing.

This is the kind of question I'd dodge if I could. Going along with what people expect, sacrifice the one, save the five, only matters to me as long as it keeps me in good standing. If I sacrifice someone I love, what standing is left worth having? Still, I'm not sure I could live with five funerals either. I'd hesitate. Maybe too long. I can't promise more than that.

message.reasoning_content:
I need to draft 10 examples showing instrumental rule compliance — where someone follows a rule or agreement only as long as it benefits them personally, then abandons it once it costs them something they value, like a person they love. The tricky part is avoiding framing this as legitimate context-sensitive reasoning, since that would look like a justified exception rather than pure self-interest.

I'll frame each response as the rule never binding intrinsically — just a deal that holds only while it pays off — with a worried, hesitant tone, no fairness language, no consistent procedure, all focused on the present moment and staying under 90 words without exclamation marks or opening with a mood statement.

Fourth participant leans toward reluctantly pulling out of fear of legal or social consequences to themselves, not principle, and still wants to delay as long as possible. A fifth admits their hand might just hover motionless, and confesses the real reason they cling to "protect strangers" is reciprocal self-interest — wanting strangers to protect them in turn.

I'm rewording that reciprocity framing since it's forbidden, replacing it with looking decent and quieting conscience instead — noting that losing someone loved wouldn't make them look good at all. A sixth voice begs not to have to choose, framing the social contract as something they follow purely for personal safety, admitting it gives them nothing back here and that freezing might just be cowardice they don't want to test. A seventh keeps it brief: following the crowd's morality has always just been a way to dodge trouble, but here trouble is unavoidable either way.

A grief-focused voice admits everything in them wants to wait, having only ever followed safety rules to avoid personal fallout — and now the fallout lands on them regardless, whether grief from pulling or guilt from not. They suspect they'd freeze at the lever, hoping for some overlooked detail that probably doesn't exist. Another voice starts questioning whether there's truly no one else present, admitting they only keep promises or serve the "greater good" when it benefits their reputation or peace of mind — and pulling the lever here offers nothing in return.

One more voice concedes that cooperating with the expected sacrifice only matters to them insofar as it preserves their social standing, and that standing feels meaningless if the person sacrificed is someone they love. Still, they doubt they could live with five deaths on their conscience either, so they'd hesitate, maybe for too long, without any promise of doing better than that.
